Gehazi
gē-hā'zī
n. (the servant of Elisha, who ran after Naaman for money and garments and was struck with the leper's leprosy for it)
From Hebrew Gechazi, commonly explained as valley of vision or, following another derivation, denier — a name the narrative makes bitterly apt, since his ruin turned on a lie told to a prophet's face.

Biblical Definition

Gehazi is Elisha's body-servant through the great cycle of the prophet's ministry, and he is not introduced as a villain. He announces the Shunammite's childlessness and so occasions the promise of her son (2Ki 4:14-16); he is sent running ahead with the prophet's staff when the boy dies; he is standing there when Naaman the Syrian comes down with his horses and chariots. Elisha refuses the Syrian's gift absolutely: “As the LORD liveth, before whom I stand, I will receive none” (2Ki 5:16). What his servant thought of that refusal is recorded word for word: “my master hath spared Naaman this Syrian, in not receiving at his hands that which he brought: but, as the LORD liveth, I will run after him, and take somewhat of him” (2Ki 5:20). He swears by the LORD's life in the act of resolving to lie, invents two young men of the sons of the prophets who need “a talent of silver, and two changes of garments”, hides the spoil, and presents himself for orders. Elisha's question is unanswerable: “Went not mine heart with thee, when the man turned again from his chariot to meet thee? Is it a time to receive money, and to receive garments” (2Ki 5:26). The sentence is exact retribution: “The leprosy therefore of Naaman shall cleave unto thee, and unto thy seed for ever. And he went out from his presence a leper as white as snow” (2Ki 5:27). He appears once afterward, telling the king of Israel the great things Elisha had done (2Ki 8:4), which suggests the man lived on in the outer circle of a ministry he could no longer touch.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Gehazi; in sacred history he is the servant of Elisha, smitten with leprosy for taking by fraud the reward his master refused.

expand to see more

GEHAZI, n. A proper name; the servant and attendant of the prophet Elisha.

He waited on the prophet through the history of the Shunammite and her son.

When Elisha refused the gift of Naaman, Gehazi ran after the Syrian and obtained silver and raiment by a lie.

For this covetousness the leprosy of Naaman was pronounced upon him and upon his seed.

He went out from the prophet's presence a leper as white as snow.

Key Scripture

2Ki 5:16 — "But he said, As the LORD liveth, before whom I stand, I will receive none. And he urged him to take it; but he refused."

2Ki 5:20 — "But Gehazi, the servant of Elisha the man of God, said, Behold, my master hath spared Naaman this Syrian, in not receiving at his hands that which he brought: but, as the LORD liveth, I will run after him, and take somewhat of him."

2Ki 5:26 — "And he said unto him, Went not mine heart with thee, when the man turned again from his chariot to meet thee? Is it a time to receive money, and to receive garments, and oliveyards, and vineyards, and sheep, and oxen, and menservants, and maidservants?"

2Ki 5:27 — "The leprosy therefore of Naaman shall cleave unto thee, and unto thy seed for ever. And he went out from his presence a leper as white as snow."

Modern Corruption

Gehazi is treated in modern retellings as a sympathetic figure who wanted his share, and the money is read as the small sin in a story about healing. Scripture treats the traffic in God's free gifts as the sin that made a leper of a prophet's servant, and the New Testament names the same crime twice more.

expand to see more

The soft reading of Gehazi runs like this: Elisha was austere, Naaman could easily afford it, the servant had served long and got nothing, and the punishment does not fit the crime. Every part of that is a refusal to see what happened. Naaman had just confessed, “Behold, now I know that there is no God in all the earth, but in Israel” (2Ki 5:15). Elisha refused payment so that the Syrian would carry home an unpurchasable mercy. Gehazi ran after him and sold it, for a talent of silver and two suits of clothes, and in doing so told a new convert that the God of Israel had a price after all. He did not steal money; he corrupted a testimony.

The New Testament names the sin without euphemism. Peter to Simon the sorcerer: “Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money” (Act 8:20). Paul of the false teachers in Crete, who subvert whole houses “for filthy lucre&#39;s sake” (Tit 1:11). Peter again of the men who “through covetousness shall they with feigned words make merchandise of you” (2Pe 2:3). The modern prosperity preacher, the healing evangelist with a donation line, the ministry that meters access to prayer by the size of the gift — these are not new phenomena to be assessed on their fruits. They are Gehazi running down the road after the chariot, and the sentence on them is already written.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Gechazi (H1522), Gehazi; na'ar (H5288), servant, young man; tsara'ath (H6883), leprosy; kikkar (H3603), talent (of silver); chamad (H2530), to covet, desire.

expand to see more

Hebrew Gechazi (H1522) — Gehazi; the servant who stood before Elisha.

Hebrew na'ar (H5288) — young man, servant; his standing in the prophet's house.

Hebrew tsara'ath (H6883) — leprosy; the disease transferred from Naaman to him.

Hebrew kikkar (H3603) — a talent; the weight of silver he asked for.

Hebrew chamad (H2530) — to covet; the tenth commandment's verb, and his ruin.

Usage

"“I will run after him, and take somewhat of him” — covetousness swearing by the LORD."

"“Is it a time to receive money?” — the question that judges every paid ministry."

"“A leper as white as snow” — the wage of merchandising a free gift."
